title: Job 23:1–7
context: Job answers Eliphaz, after the narrator’s heading in 23:1. Job’s first movement is not a finished theodicy but a lament and a protest: his complaint is still rebellious, God’s hand is heavy, and he wishes he knew where he might find him and come to his seat, to set his cause in order and hear an answer. Job hopes that God would listen, and that there the upright might reason with him. The speech should be heard as Job’s own, a desire for a hearing, not as a system already complete. In 42:7 the LORD will say that Job has spoken of him what is right, unlike Eliphaz and the other two friends; that later word may be remembered, but it does not turn this longing into a calm conclusion, and it is not repeated in every verse. Both traditions read the unit as Job’s plea for a meeting with God, without a party contrast over the wish itself.

verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator says, “Then Job answered,” and the words that follow, through chapter 24, are Job’s. The heading only changes the speaker after Eliphaz’s third speech. It does not yet resolve the argument.

Arminian readers take the formula as a real reply from Job, his own voice returning, not the narrator stepping in to settle the case.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the line as the book’s ordinary heading, Job now answering, the content of the answer still to be heard as his.

Both traditions name Job as the speaker from here, and they invent no contrast over the heading.

verses.text: “Even today my complaint is rebellious. His hand is heavy in spite of my groaning.
verses.arminianNotes:
Job begins, “Even today my complaint is rebellious.” God’s hand, he says, is heavy in spite of his groaning. Job himself calls the complaint rebellious, and he feels that hand as heavy even as he groans. The speaker is Job. The notes do not soften the word “rebellious” and they do not treat it as a confession that Eliphaz’s charges are true.

Arminian readers hear a man still in protest, naming the bitterness of his own complaint, while God’s hand remains heavy on him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also let Job describe his complaint as rebellious and the hand as heavy, a lament, not a retraction of his integrity.

Both traditions keep the two sentences together: protest and the weight of God’s hand, without a contrast over the wording.

verses.text: Oh that I knew where I might find him! That I might come even to his seat!
verses.arminianNotes:
“Oh that I knew where I might find him! That I might come even to his seat!” Job’s wish is to find God and to come to his seat, the place of hearing and of decision. This is lament and longing, not a map he already holds, and not a finished account of why the righteous suffer. The God he seeks is not, for him, an unknown deity; he seeks a meeting he cannot yet locate.

Arminian readers take the cry as a genuine desire for God’s presence and for a place to be heard, a free and painful seeking, not a proof that God is absent as if he were not there at all.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a real longing to find God and to come to his seat, Job still addressing the God who is, even while he does not know where to come at him.

Both traditions refuse to turn “where I might find him” into a doctrine of God’s actual absence, and they invent no contrast over the wish.

verses.text: I would set my cause in order before him, and fill my mouth with arguments.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I would set my cause in order before him, and fill my mouth with arguments.” If he found that seat, Job would order his case and speak arguments. Job wants a legal hearing, not a silence. The arguments are not spelled out here; the desire for them is.

Arminian readers take the planned cause as Job’s serious intention to speak, a real wish to be heard in order, not a threat of empty debate.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the cause and the arguments as Job’s hoped-for speech before God, the protest of a man who still wants a hearing rather than a last word already in hand.

Both traditions leave the arguments unnamed, as Job does, and invent no contrast over the legal language.

verses.text: I would know the words which he would answer me, and understand what he would tell me.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I would know the words which he would answer me, and understand what he would tell me.” Job wants not only to speak but to hear and understand God’s answer. The meeting he seeks is two-sided. Job does not claim already to have that answer; he wishes he could know it.

Arminian readers hear a genuine openness to being answered, a desire to understand what God would say, not a demand that God submit to Job’s terms in advance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the hoped-for words as Job’s longing for a real reply from God, understanding still ahead of him, not in his hand.

Both traditions keep the verse as a plea for an answer, not as a finished theodicy.

verses.text: Would he contend with me in the greatness of his power? No, but he would listen to me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Job asks, “Would he contend with me in the greatness of his power? No, but he would listen to me.” Job both fears the inequality of power and, in the same breath, trusts that God would listen rather than merely overpower him. The “No” is Job’s own hope, spoken in the midst of complaint, not a doctrine already proved by the event.

Arminian readers hear a trust that God would listen, a hope about the character of the hearing Job cannot yet find, held together with the fear of God’s power.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also let the question and the “No” stand: Job does not expect a contest of raw force, and he hopes to be heard. The hope is his, and it is not yet the scene of later chapters imported here.

Both traditions refuse to flatten the verse into either simple confidence or simple despair.

verses.text: There the upright might reason with him, so I should be delivered forever from my judge.
verses.arminianNotes:
“There the upright might reason with him, so I should be delivered forever from my judge.” Job pictures a place where the upright can reason with God, and he hopes for a lasting deliverance from his judge. Job still calls God his judge. The hope is real, and it remains a hope there, at the seat he has not found. It should not be read as a claim that the trial is already over.

Arminian readers take the reasoning of the upright as Job’s conviction that a fair hearing with God is possible, and the deliverance as what he seeks, not what he already holds.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear Job still naming God as judge, and still hoping that there, if he could come, the upright might reason and he would be delivered.

Both traditions keep the verse in the register of longing, and they invent no contrast over the hope of being heard.
